clue.text: Likes to include piece of music in gymnastic exercise

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one word holds the other within it

blocks.note: likes as a noun: things that match or correspond to one another
a bar is a short measured section of a score

explanation.surface: A gymnast performs a floor routine set to a favourite piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Likes' is the plural noun, as in 'the likes of', meaning counterparts, not the verb of fondness.
explanation.definitionFit: The parallel bars are an apparatus event in men's artistic gymnastics, so the routine performed on them counts as an exercise.

clue.text: Moving picture about husband and love? His love’s considered a handful

indicators.note: something moving will not stay in place, so these letters are shifted into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the standard abbreviation for husband
love is zero in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A film about a married couple, with a husband whose wife is hard to manage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving picture' looks like a film, but 'Moving' rearranges the letters of 'picture' together with H and O.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, Petruchio woos and marries Katherina, the notoriously difficult shrew of the title.

clue.text: Storm enveloping two-thirds of more unsettled star

indicators.note: keeping only two parts in three means the final third of the word is dropped
to envelop is to wrap around, so one word surrounds the other

blocks.note: to storm is to rage or rant noisily
edgy means nervous or unsettled; EDGIER is the comparative

explanation.surface: A gathering storm makes a nervous celebrity even more jittery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' looks like a celebrity in the surface, but it is the astronomical kind. Two-thirds of a six-letter word means its first four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A red giant is a large, cool, luminous star in a late stage of its life, so it is one kind of star.

clue.text: Minimum area, small, included in rent

indicators.note: being included in something means sitting inside it, so these letters go within another word

blocks.note: to let a property is to rent it out
A is the standard abbreviation for area
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A tenant pays rent for the smallest possible floor space.
explanation.walkthrough: A and S go together inside LET, splitting it after the E.
explanation.definitionFit: Least and minimum both describe the smallest possible amount, so the adjective can stand in for the noun used attributively.

clue.text: Corrupt empires imprisoning the man producing almanac

indicators.note: something corrupt has been spoiled from its proper form, so these letters are mangled into a new order
to imprison is to lock inside, so one word is enclosed by another

blocks.note: taken as written
a man is referred to as he

explanation.surface: Corrupt imperial powers jail a man who publishes a yearly almanac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almanac' suggests a farmer's yearbook, but this one is astronomical; the man goes in after the rearranged letters' first two.
explanation.definitionFit: An ephemeris is a table or book giving the predicted positions of heavenly bodies, a kind of astronomical almanac.

clue.text: Minor official’s bottom, pornographic, not for the refined?

indicators.note: U stands for upper class, the refined set, so removing what is for them means dropping that letter

blocks.note: bum is British slang for the buttocks
a blue film or joke is a smutty one

explanation.surface: A petty bureaucrat's backside appears in smutty material unsuitable for polite company.
explanation.walkthrough: U is crossword shorthand for upper class or refined, so it leaves BLUE. Mr Bumble is the pompous parish beadle in Dickens's Oliver Twist, whose name gave English 'bumbledom'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bumble, from the Dickens beadle, is a dictionary word for a self-important petty official, which fits a minor functionary.

clue.text: Fashion bringing in new collection of styles

indicators.note: to bring something in is to take it inside, so a letter is placed within the word

blocks.note: the rage is the current craze, as in 'all the rage'
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A fashion house launches a new collection of styles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' reads as a verb or the clothing industry, but here it is a noun meaning craze.
explanation.definitionFit: A range is a set of related products from one maker, such as a line of clothing in different designs.

clue.text: Discussion implying support for right-wing views?

blocks.note: Con is short for Conservative, the British right-of-centre party
fab, short for fabulous, is a cry of enthusiastic approval

explanation.surface: A debate that hints at sympathy with conservative opinions.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'Con? Fab!', a cheer for the Conservatives; the order of the pieces follows that cheer, not the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A confab, short for confabulation, is an informal chat or conference, so it is a casual synonym for a talk.

clue.text: Simple creature, nameless one in possession of a business degree? On the contrary

indicators.note: without a name means losing the abbreviation for name, so a letter drops out
to possess is to hold, so one piece is held inside another
the contrary of the stated arrangement swaps which part holds and which is held

blocks.note: taken as written
the Master of Business Administration
taken as written; N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: An unnamed simpleton boasts an MBA, or perhaps the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, OE would hold A MBA; 'On the contrary' reverses the roles, so A MBA holds OE.
explanation.definitionFit: An amoeba is a single-celled organism, the textbook example of the most basic form of animal life.

clue.text: Brought on board after failing company made a decision

indicators.note: failing here means lacking or in the absence of, so something is taken away

blocks.note: to co-opt is to appoint someone to a board or committee by the existing members' vote
CO is the standard abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: After a firm collapsed, a new director was appointed and a choice was made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing company' looks like a struggling business; here 'failing' means without, removing CO from the front of COOPTED.
explanation.definitionFit: To opt is to choose between alternatives, so the past tense means someone chose or decided.

clue.text: Are reckless Don and him (EM) attacking opponents’ characters?

indicators.note: reckless behaviour is wild and careless, so the letters that follow are thrown about

blocks.note: an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated A
the three words taken as written

explanation.surface: Are Don and the other man rashly smearing their rivals?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are' looks like the verb but is the metric unit of 100 square metres. The odd '(EM)' is just more letters for the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An ad hominem argument targets the person rather than the reasoning, so it means going after the other side's character.

clue.text: Colour not on visual spectrum, one adopted by dissolute artist

indicators.note: being adopted means being taken into a family, so these letters are taken inside another word

blocks.note: fast in the old sense of loose-living or dissipated
ultraviolet light lies beyond the visible spectrum
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A debauched painter takes up a colour nobody can see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colour' only sets the scene: the Fauves were known for wild, vivid colour. Ultraviolet is invisible to the human eye, hence its place here.
explanation.definitionFit: A Fauvist was a painter of the early 1900s movement led by Matisse, so the word names a particular kind of artist.

clue.text: Playwright increasingly accepting story

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one word receives the other inside it

blocks.note: more and more, to a growing degree
a story is a fib or untruth

explanation.surface: A dramatist is becoming ever more willing to take on a tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'story' is a fib here, not a narrative.
explanation.definitionFit: Molière was the seventeenth-century French comic dramatist who wrote Tartuffe and The Misanthrope.

clue.text: Places for mixologists in prison?

definitions.note: a noun phrase for a phrase that works as a location

blocks.note: first meaning: where cocktail makers work, serving across the counter
second meaning: locked up in a cell

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests cocktail bartenders in jail; the joke is that the bartender's ordinary workplace phrase is the idiom for being jailed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bartenders literally stand behind the bar counter, while the idiom for imprisonment refers to the metal grilles of a cell.

clue.text: Summer clothing to support accommodating every individual width

indicators.note: to accommodate is to house or make room for, so one word has others placed inside it

blocks.note: to bear a weight is to support it
each refers to every single one
W is the abbreviation for width

explanation.surface: Lightweight summer clothing needs to fit people of every size and width.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summer clothing to support' reads as one phrase, but the definition ends at 'clothing' and 'to' simply joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Beachwear covers swimsuits, sarongs and other garments worn at the seaside, typically in the warm months.

clue.text: City each year filled with heartless Italians?

indicators.note: without a heart, a word loses its whole middle and keeps only its two ends
something filled has contents put inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: p.a. is per annum, Latin for each year
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Every year an Italian city is packed with unfeeling locals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' sounds like a judgment on the Italians, but it strips the word down to its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Pisa is a city in Tuscany, famous for its leaning bell tower, so it is a specific example of a city.

clue.text: Contract, one getting navy a lot of choppers?

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
N is the abbreviation for navy
choppers is slang for teeth, and a denture is a set of false ones

explanation.surface: A deal for one supplier to provide the navy with many helicopters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'choppers' suggests helicopters for the navy, but it is slang for teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: An indenture is a formal legal agreement, especially one binding an apprentice to a master, so it is a type of contract.

clue.text: Animal perversion a Judge banned? Not entirely

indicators.note: not the entire word means it stops short, losing its last letter

blocks.note: a kink is an unusual sexual taste
taken as written
J is the abbreviation for judge
something banned is out, not permitted

explanation.surface: A judge outlaws a sexual deviation involving animals, though only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely' looks like a comment on the ban, but it clips the final letter from OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: The kinkajou is a tree-dwelling mammal of Central and South American rainforests, related to the raccoon.

clue.text: Time right to bring in new revolutionary measure of speed

indicators.note: bringing something in puts it inside, so a letter is placed within the others
a revolution turns things round, so the whole assembly is turned back to front

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
OK means correct or all right
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: The time is right to introduce a radical new way of measuring speed.
explanation.walkthrough: T and OK make TOK; N goes inside to give TONK, which then turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: A knot is one nautical mile per hour, the unit used for the speed of ships and aircraft.

clue.text: Some glamorous babe keeps up the cooked meat

definitions.note: singular collective phrase for a plural answer

indicators.note: taking only some of the words means the letters are found inside them
in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of the first word to the start of the third

explanation.surface: A glamorous woman stays up late eating takeaway meat.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'glamorous', 'babe' and 'keeps'; 'up' tells you to read them upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Kebabs are pieces of meat grilled or roasted on a skewer or spit, so they are cooked meat dishes.

clue.text: Member of orchestra having fish served with trifle

blocks.note: the bass is a spiny-finned food fish
to trifle or fiddle is to fidget or toy idly with something

explanation.surface: An orchestral musician dines on fish followed by a custard dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trifle' looks like the British layered pudding of sponge, fruit, custard and cream, but it is the verb meaning to toy with.
explanation.definitionFit: The bass fiddle is an informal name for the double bass, the lowest-pitched string instrument in a symphony orchestra.

clue.text: Substitute located in the heart of Germany? Not initially

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so these letters go within another word
without its start, a word loses its first letter

blocks.note: Herz is the German word for heart
something that sat somewhere was situated or located there

explanation.surface: A replacement found somewhere in central Germany, though not at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the heart of Germany' tempts you to take the middle letters of the country's name; instead it asks for the German for heart, HERZ, which loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz, borrowed from German, describes an inferior imitation used in place of the real thing, so it means a substitute.

clue.text: Stunning item about Pasquale’s latest puzzle

indicators.note: the latest of anything is the final one, so only the closing letter is taken
about means around, so one word is wrapped round the other

blocks.note: a Taser is an electric stun gun
the final letter of the setter's name

explanation.surface: A stunning feature in the newest crossword by the Guardian setter Pasquale.
explanation.walkthrough: Pasquale is a fellow Guardian setter, so the surface praises a colleague's work; 'Stunning' means delivering a shock, not impressive.
explanation.definitionFit: A teaser, short for brainteaser, is a tricky problem or riddle set to test the solver, a kind of puzzle.

clue.text: Life tutor ignoring a source of green energy?

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out of account, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: bio is the combining form meaning life
to tutor is to teach
taken as written

explanation.surface: A life coach dismisses a renewable power supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Life tutor' suggests a coach, but 'tutor' is a verb here, and the question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Biotechnology produces biofuels from crops and algae, so it can be offered as one possible origin of renewable power.

clue.text: Speak in great detail, forgetting note

indicators.note: what is forgotten is left out, so a letter goes missing

blocks.note: ornate means elaborately decorated, full of fine detail
N is an abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: Someone talks at great length about every detail but forgets one point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speak in great detail' looks like a single instruction, but the definition stops at 'Speak'.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to deliver a formal speech, often pompously, so it is a verb for public speaking.

clue.text: Cheers monarch going to Southern gate

blocks.note: ta is British informal for thanks
a king is a monarch
S is the abbreviation for southern

explanation.surface: Crowds cheer as the king heads for the south gate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gate' reads as an entrance, but in sport it is the money taken from spectators at a match.
explanation.definitionFit: A gate is the total receipts from admission at an event, and takings are the money collected by a business.

clue.text: Article on limits of weakness or strength

indicators.note: the limits of something are its boundaries, so only its two end letters are used

blocks.note: the definite article
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A piece of writing on the extremes of frailty or might.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' means placed above, so THE sits on top of the two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Thews is an old literary word for muscles or sinews, and by extension for bodily power and vigour.

clue.text: Bar moving one supporter

indicators.note: shifting a single letter to another place rearranges the word into a new order

blocks.note: a brasserie is a bar or informal restaurant

explanation.surface: A bar relocating one of its loyal patrons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' is I, the Roman numeral: move the I in BRASSERIE two places forward. 'supporter' suggests a fan of the bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A brassiere is an undergarment that holds up the breasts, so it is literally a supporting garment.

clue.text: Deserved to bag round in fight

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it in a sack, so a letter is held inside

blocks.note: just means fair or deserved, as in just deserts
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A boxer earned the right to win a round of the bout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' sounds like a stage in a boxing match, but it is the circular letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A joust is a mounted combat between knights with lances, so it is a medieval form of armed contest.

clue.text: Strain to see Trump, say, having certain behaviour found in groups

blocks.note: to peer is to look hard, straining the eyes
Trump is an example of a US president, shortened to PRES
sure means certain

explanation.surface: People squint to watch Trump, who has distinctive habits shared by his followers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks Trump as just one example of a president.
explanation.definitionFit: Peer pressure is the social influence that makes members of a group conform to its habits and attitudes.
